lead: Most accidents afloat are ordinary: a fall, a burn, a gas leak, a propeller near a swimmer. The skipper makes them unlikely and keeps gear and crew ready.

qa.q: What lifejacket rating do I need for coastal sailing, and how should I wear it?
qa.a: 150 N is the minimum for coastal and offshore sailing. Wear it as the outer layer, waist belt snug and **crotch strap** fastened, or it rides up over your face.

blocks.p: Carry a lifejacket of the right size for everyone aboard; a child's goes by weight. Wear it as the outer layer, waist belt snug and **crotch strap** fastened, or it rides up over your face. An automatic one inflates even if you are knocked out. In breaking waves pull down its sprayhood.
At check-in look inside each: cylinder tight and unfired, indicators green. Replace any extinguisher whose gauge is in the red.

sections.title: Clip on before you need it

qa.q: When should I clip on my harness on a sailing yacht, and to what?
qa.a: At night or in a fresh wind, clip on before leaving the companionway, to a strong point or the **jackstay**, never a guardrail, on a tether too short to reach the water.

blocks.p: At night or in a fresh wind everyone on deck wears a lifejacket and clips on: before leaving the companionway, to a strong point or the **jackstay**, never a guardrail, on a tether too short to reach the water. Clip the second hook on before releasing the first. Alone on watch at night you stay clipped on.

fig.note: Dead run: rig a preventer, heads below the boom

blocks.p: Go forward on the windward side, low, one hand for the boat. Keep limbs out from between boat and quay, hands off the windlass. Use the heads, not the rail. At night use red light below, tell the helm before going forward, and wake the skipper early.

fig.note: Shout, throw the buoys, point, press MOB

blocks.p: Never tie down the danbuoy and horseshoe: they must go in seconds.

qa.q: Which extinguisher goes on which fire aboard, and what do I do if I smell gas?
qa.a: Match it to what burns: a fire blanket on a pan of oil, powder or foam on fuel, CO2 or powder on electrics, never water on oil or fuel. Smell **gas**? No flames, no switches: shut the bottle and ventilate.

blocks.p: Hang the fire blanket beside the cooker, not above it, and show everyone the escape hatches.

**Gas** is heavier than air: a leak sinks into the bilge, where a spark ignites it. So bottles live in a locker draining overboard, the alarm sensor sits low, and the valve is open only while you cook. Smell gas? No flames, no switches: shut the bottle, ventilate, pump the bilge by hand. Test joints with soapy water. Petrol too stays outside the hull.

lines: No smell, nobody feels ill yet

blocks.p: **Carbon monoxide** from an exhaust has no smell: headache and nausea below mean fresh air at once and medical advice. At sea, strap the cook in, clamp the pans, let the stove swing.

qa.q: When should we actually get into the liferaft if the yacht is in trouble?
qa.a: Only when the yacht is sinking: she is your best lifeboat, so you step up into the raft from her. Until then keep the raft ready on deck, its painter made fast.

blocks.p: The yacht is your best lifeboat: step up into the raft only when she is sinking; until then keep it ready on deck, painter made fast. A raft must be in date and quick to launch. Its **hydrostatic release** lets it float free and inflate, unless someone has lashed it down.

blocks.p: The **grab bag** waits by the companionway: handheld VHF in a waterproof pouch, flares, torch, first aid, and water in small, part-filled bottles that float.

qa.q: What first aid do I give for a burn or hypothermia on a sailing trip?
qa.a: Cool a burn under running water for 20 minutes, then cover it loosely with cling film. Handle someone with **hypothermia** gently: lay them flat, insulate them and warm them slowly, with no alcohol.

blocks.p: Before sailing, ask the crew about conditions, allergies and medicines.

blocks.p: **Seasickness**: tablets before sailing, then fresh air, the helm and the horizon; be sick to leeward, clipped on. A day of vomiting without keeping water down is serious. Anyone who has inhaled water sees a doctor that day.

sections.title: Propellers and swimmers do not mix

qa.q: How do I use the tender safely when people are swimming near the yacht?
qa.a: Wear the outboard's **kill cord** on your leg or lifejacket, so the engine stops if you fall out, and start it in neutral with swimmers well clear. Before anyone swims from the yacht, stop her engine.

blocks.p: In the tender wear the **kill cord** on your leg or lifejacket: fall out and the engine stops. Obey the builder's plate. Carry oars, a bailer and a phone in a dry bag; at night a torch, lifejackets and a sober driver. Start the outboard in neutral, swimmers well clear, and keep a safety line on it until clamped on.

fig.note: Y: your yacht, 300 m off the beach

blocks.p: Before anyone swims, stop the engine and lower the ladder. Stream a floating line astern. Swimming ashore needs a bright tow float and a route clear of tenders. Nobody swims after drinking or in the dark.

qa.q: What should a skipper cover in the safety briefing before leaving harbour?
qa.a: The **safety briefing** covers lifejackets, gas, heads, fire, man overboard, VHF and flares. Someone besides the skipper must be able to stop the boat, use the VHF and start the MOB drill.

blocks.p: You answer for everyone aboard, so your safety rules stand. Before leaving, give the **safety briefing**: lifejackets, gas, heads, fire, man overboard, VHF, flares. Someone else must be able to stop the boat, use the VHF and start the MOB drill. Whoever steers or keeps watch stays off alcohol.

On passage set watches so that everyone sleeps, you included, each led by someone experienced, and nobody drowsy from tablets alone. Tell the crew the plan. Tired, with an unlit harbour ahead? Wait offshore for daylight.
